technique: the exit — leaving on an image instead of a statement
lesson: Today we work on one technique. Call it the exit. The exit means the poem spends its last lines on a picture of a thing, not on a conclusion the poet tells you. Most of this poem is pictures. But look at how it actually ends. It stops on a flat instruction: "get out there and let it." That is a statement, not a picture. So I want you to watch the strongest picture it leaves you with before that: "a woman's name warm in the week ahead like a coal banked for Friday." A banked coal is a fire kept low overnight so it still burns in the morning. That line sticks because you can almost feel heat. A picture lasts in your memory longer than a command does. Try this: end your poem one line sooner, on the last thing a person could see or touch. The second time through, listen for that coal line and notice how much it carries. Here is the poem.
poem:
The fog that sat the valley overnight
pulls up off the low ground like a sheet
drawn back from something that was only sleeping,
and the wind comes next, working the bare tops
with a sound like water that isn't there.
The last of the rain stands in the wheel-ruts,
holding a little sky it hasn't spilled yet.
You pull your collar up and the cold goes honest,
no arguing with it, the brush set down for the year,
the ledger squared, a woman's name warm
in the week ahead like a coal banked for Friday.

The day's already leaning toward you—
get out there and let it.
